rows.gold_para: Early studies pointed to fascinating features of Acanthamoeba mitochondria. Although it is a “cousin” of animals and fungi, its circular mtDNA encodes an impressive 42 open reading frames (ORFs)32–35 in comparison to 13 in humans36 and eight conserved mtDNA ORFs in yeast.37 Acanthamoeba contains a superset of mitochondrial pathways found in humans and yeast, including: (i) a full OXPHOS system spanning complex I–V,33,35,38–40 (ii) an ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES)41, (iii) an uncoupling protein (UCP)42, (iv) three type II NADH dehydrogenases (NDH2s)43 (found in yeast but absent in humans), and (v) an alternative oxidase (AOX),44,45 which is absent in humans and in yeast. In addition, prior genome analysis suggested Acanthamoeba may possess pathways for anerobic ATP production not present in yeast or animals. These include [FeFe]-hydrogenase (HydA) and its assembly factors (HydE, HydF, HydG), pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR), and acetate:succinate CoA transferase 1B (ASCT1B), which is important for anaerobic ATP production via substrate-level phosphorylation.46 While mitochondrial localization has been predicted,46 definitive subcellular localization of these enzymes, their assembly factors, and their activities is still lacking. Neither Acanthamoeba cells nor their isolated mitochondria have been shown to generate or consume H2. It also remains unclear whether these pathways and their activities are constitutively active or environmentally regulated.

While these ingredients can visibly improve wrinkles, uneven tone, and texture, they mostly address downstream manifestations of aging rather than its underlying biological drivers.
